notes: No political parties exist in Western Samoa in 1970 (HRPP only founded 1979, so not used). Ruling slot 1 holds Fa'amatai, the matai system that elects the Assembly and backs the Fiame Mata'afa cabinet; head of state Malietoa Tanumafili II leads it. Slot 2 (coalition partner) holds the Individual Voters' Roll (2 Assembly seats). Slot 23 follows MD: O le Ao o le Malo. No army, so slot 22 is the police.

0.name: Feagaiga ma Niu Sila
0.text:
Feagaiga ma Niu Sila gathers the senior matai, civil servants and New Zealand-trained officials who regard the 1962 Treaty of Friendship as the bedrock of the state. Wellington still handles much of Apia's diplomacy, seconds advisers to ministries and funds schools and hospitals, and this circle around Prime Minister Fiame Mata'afa's cabinet treats that relationship as untouchable. It prefers quiet government by chiefs and experts to open contest.

The group wants order, aid and a firm Western anchor: New Zealand protection, Australian and American goodwill, and no adventures with Moscow or Beijing. Its leverage lies in the aid pipeline, in scholarships to New Zealand and in the expatriate advisers who draft much of the government's development planning.

1.name: Fa'amatai
1.text:
Fa'amatai, the system of chiefly titles, is the government of Western Samoa in all but name. Only matai may vote for or sit in 45 of the 47 seats of the Legislative Assembly, and the cabinet of Prime Minister Fiame Mata'afa, himself holder of one of the four paramount titles, rests on their consensus. Head of State Malietoa Tanumafili II stands above it as its highest guardian. No political parties exist; loyalty runs through families, villages and districts.

The matai defend fa'a Samoa: customary land that cannot be sold, village councils that keep order, and the churches that bless both. They welcome Western aid and friendship with New Zealand but resist universal suffrage, party politics and anything that would loosen the authority of titled heads over their families.

2.name: Individual Voters' Roll
2.text:
The Individual Voters' Roll is the separate electorate for citizens of European and part-Samoan descent who live outside the matai system. Concentrated in Apia's commercial quarter, they elect two members to the Legislative Assembly and dominate trade, the professions and the senior ranks of the public service. Families descended from nineteenth-century traders and planters give the roll its leading names.

Its members favour individual property rights, a freer land market, commercial law and a professional bureaucracy, and many quietly sympathise with universal suffrage and organised parties. They are firmly pro-Western, tied to New Zealand and Australian firms and banks. Their influence rests on money, education and fluency in English, not on numbers.

3.name: Public Service Association
3.text:
The Public Service Association represents the clerks, teachers, nurses and technicians who staff the government departments at Mulinu'u and Apia. It is the closest thing Western Samoa has to a trade union: a small, salaried, English-educated membership that bargains over pay and conditions with the Public Service Commission and looks to the New Zealand labour movement as its model.

The association is cautious and loyal, but it carries a social-democratic outlook: wage scales tied to living costs, pensions, public health and schooling for all, and a government answerable to more than the matai. It is pro-Western and anti-communist. Its leverage lies in the simple fact that the state cannot run without its members.

4.name: Tagata Faigaluega o Apia
4.text:
Tagata Faigaluega o Apia is a handful of wharf hands, plantation labourers and returned migrants who met socialist ideas in the factories and union halls of Auckland and Wellington. There is no communist party in Western Samoa and the churches would not tolerate one; the circle meets privately, passes around pamphlets from New Zealand's pro-Soviet Socialist Unity Party, and avoids the attention of police and village councils.

Its members denounce the plantation economy, the commercial houses of Apia and the matai monopoly on the vote, and hold up the Soviet Union as proof that poor nations can industrialise. They call for trade unions, universal suffrage and land for the untitled. Their only real asset is the growing number of Samoans working abroad.

5.name: Tupulaga Fou
5.text:
Tupulaga Fou is the restless mood of young Samoans who have studied at Samoa College, in New Zealand or at the new University of the South Pacific in Suva. Exposed to campus protest against the Vietnam War, apartheid sport and colonialism, they return to villages where the untitled have no vote and elders decide everything. They have no leader and no organisation beyond student clubs and church youth groups.

They demand universal suffrage, an end to the matai franchise, solidarity with liberation movements and less dependence on New Zealand. Their radicalism targets gerontocracy and church authority as much as foreign influence. Their leverage is demographic: half the population is young, and more of the young now earn wages abroad.

6.name: Tumua ma Pule
6.text:
Tumua and Pule are the ancient orator centres of Upolu and Savai'i, the traditional voice of all Samoa long before the constitution. In the days of the Mau they spoke for the nation against New Zealand rule, and their orators still claim the right to confer the highest titles and to judge whether a government acts according to custom.

In 1970 they stand for hardline tradition: suspicion of foreign advisers, Western commerce and imported ideas, and insistence that the state answer to fa'a Samoa rather than to Wellington. They oppose universal suffrage and the registration of customary land. Their leverage is moral and ceremonial, but no title dispute or national ceremony can ignore them.

7.name: Malo Malosi
7.text:
Malo Malosi is the outlook of ministers, district officials and senior matai who think independence has left Western Samoa too dependent and too slow. They admire the decisive rule of other new states and resent the advisers, aid conditions and commercial houses that tie Apia to New Zealand and Australia. The faction has no organisation of its own and works inside the cabinet and the public service.

Its adherents want a strong executive that can override village objections, take control of trade and plantations, and seek aid and markets wherever they are offered, including from the Soviet bloc. They distrust the press and the courts. Their leverage depends on capturing the prime minister's office.

8.name: Halqat Ahl al-Bayt
8.text:
Halqat Ahl al-Bayt is a tiny gathering of Muslim seamen and traders from Fiji and the Indian Ocean who pass through Apia's port and occasionally meet for prayer and study. A few of them follow Shia teaching through contacts with Khoja communities in India and East Africa. Western Samoa has no mosque and no registered Muslim body.

The circle shares the outlook of reformist Shia clergy such as Musa al-Sadr in Lebanon: faith tied to social justice, education and dignity for the poor, with respect for local law and religious pluralism. It has no political ambitions on the islands. Its significance lies only in the links it keeps to a much larger Muslim world.

9.name: Ansar al-Najaf
9.text:
Ansar al-Najaf is the name a few Shia sailors and students give to their loyalty to the exiled Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, whose lectures on Islamic government circulate from Najaf. In Western Samoa their presence is negligible: a handful of transient believers with recordings and pamphlets carried along the Pacific shipping lanes.

They hold that legitimate rule belongs to the Islamic jurist, condemn both American and Soviet power, and see Christian missions and the Western-backed order in the Pacific as forms of domination. They have no base among Samoans. Any influence would depend on a revolution in the Muslim heartlands that gives their cause money and prestige.

10.name: Rabitat al-'Alam al-Islami
10.text:
The Muslim World League, founded in Mecca in 1962 under Saudi royal patronage, sends literature, scholarships and occasional preachers to Muslim communities across the Pacific, mostly through Fiji. In Western Samoa it reaches only the few Muslim traders and seamen in Apia and the odd convert who corresponds with its offices.

The League preaches a Saudi-sponsored orthodoxy: loyalty to Muslim rulers, strict monotheism, opposition to communism and secular nationalism, and close ties to the West against Soviet influence. It builds mosques and schools rather than parties. Its leverage is money: should a Muslim community ever form here, it would be the first patron to fund it.

11.name: Da'wat al-Khilafa
11.text:
Da'wat al-Khilafa is the idea of a restored caliphate as carried by Hizb ut-Tahrir pamphlets and by a few Muslim students who meet them at universities in New Zealand, Australia and Fiji. In Western Samoa there is no organised following, only scattered readers among foreign workers and the rare Samoan convert.

The circle rejects nation-states, democracy and monarchy alike as man-made systems, and calls for a single Islamic state under one caliph that would sweep away both Western and Soviet influence. It is secretive by habit and hostile to established Muslim leaders. It has no leverage in a Christian society beyond the curiosity of a few disaffected young people.

12.name: New Zealand Muslim Association
12.text:
The New Zealand Muslim Association, founded in Auckland in 1950 by Indian and European Muslims, is the nearest organised Muslim body to Western Samoa. As Samoan migration to Auckland grows, a few Samoans encounter it through workplaces and marriages, and Muslim visitors to Apia carry its literature and contacts.

The association combines prayer, charity and education with a modern outlook shaped by South Asian and Arab revivalism: Islamic ethics in public life, mutual aid and lawful participation in politics. It is anti-communist and works within Western democratic institutions. Its leverage in Western Samoa runs entirely through the migrant link with Auckland.

13.name: Public Service Commission
13.text:
The Public Service Commission appoints, promotes and disciplines Western Samoa's civil servants. Built on New Zealand practice before independence, it still relies on expatriate officers and New Zealand-trained Samoans who see themselves as the guardians of competent, neutral government in a state without parties.

Its senior officials favour planning, statistics and administrative order over the bargaining of chiefs and villages: development plans, regulated trade, state enterprises and careful use of foreign aid from any donor. They are neither ideological nor aligned, but believe government should be run by experts. Their leverage lies in controlling the machinery on which every cabinet depends.

14.name: Ekalesia Fa'apotopotoga Kerisiano Samoa
14.text:
The Congregational Christian Church in Samoa grew from the London Missionary Society mission that arrived in 1830 and became an independent Samoan church in 1962. It is the largest denomination in the country, present in almost every village, and its pastors stand beside the matai at the centre of village life.

The church upholds Sunday observance, family discipline, the authority of chiefs and the moral leadership of the clergy. It is wary of secular ideologies from either bloc and of rapid social change, but supports schools, scholarships and development. Its leverage is immense: congregations raise funds, form opinion and lend legitimacy to any government that respects them.

15.name: Western Samoa Trust Estates Corporation
15.text:
The Western Samoa Trust Estates Corporation holds the former German plantations seized by New Zealand in 1914 and handed to the Samoan state in 1957. Its cocoa, copra and cattle estates make it the country's largest landowner and employer, and its board brings together senior politicians, Apia merchants and expatriate managers.

The corporation stands for export earnings, plantation discipline and the commercial interests of the Apia establishment. Its directors resist land redistribution to villages and wage militancy, and favour close ties to New Zealand and Australian markets. Its leverage comes from controlling the best freehold land, foreign exchange and patronage jobs across Upolu.

16.name: Burns Philp
16.text:
Burns Philp, the Sydney-based shipping and trading company, runs one of the main import and copra-buying businesses in Apia alongside a few Samoan and part-Samoan merchant houses. Its stores, ships and credit reach into villages across Upolu and Savai'i, and its managers sit at the heart of the town's commercial community.

The firm and the traders around it want low tariffs, free movement of goods and capital, open copra buying instead of state boards, and secure commercial law. They distrust government enterprise and favour Australia and New Zealand as partners. Their leverage lies in credit and supply: villages, shops and even ministries depend on what their ships bring in.

17.name: Fanua ma le Sami
17.text:
Fanua ma le Sami brings together village councils, pastors and fishermen alarmed by the felling of Savai'i's forests, the dynamiting of reefs and the spread of plantations onto customary land. Its concern is old: Samoans see land and lagoon as held in trust for future generations. It has no formal organisation and works through district councils and church meetings.

It wants customary land kept out of the market, logging concessions restricted, reef fishing protected from destructive methods, and development that leaves the village intact. It is suspicious of foreign timber and plantation companies whatever their flag. Its leverage lies in village councils, which can halt projects on their land.

18.name: Komiti Tumama
18.text:
The Komiti Tumama, the women's health committees set up under New Zealand rule in the 1920s and now found in nearly every village, are the most effective grassroots network in Western Samoa. Led by the wives of matai and pastors, they run clinics, inspect sanitation, raise funds for water supplies and schools, and work closely with district nurses.

Their outlook is communal welfare rather than ideology: public health, education, village cooperation and fair access to development money. They are non-aligned, pragmatic and suspicious of both commercial exploitation and radical politics. Their leverage comes from organisation and fundraising; ministries rely on them to deliver programmes in the villages.

19.name: Aumaga Mumu
19.text:
Aumaga Mumu is a loose circle of untitled young men and returned workers who have absorbed Maoist ideas in New Zealand, where the Communist Party of New Zealand sides with Beijing. The aumaga, the village body of untitled men who do the heavy work of the community, gives them both their name and their grievance.

They see the matai as a feudal class, the Apia merchants as compradors and the aid relationship with New Zealand as neocolonialism. They call for land to the tillers, rule by village assemblies of all adults and self-reliance on the Chinese model, rejecting Soviet revisionism as well. They are tiny, but their language echoes among frustrated untitled men.

20.name: Samoa mo Samoa
20.text:
Samoa mo Samoa takes its name from the old slogan of the Mau, the mass movement that defied New Zealand rule in the 1920s and 1930s. Its heirs are matai and orators, many from families once active in the Mau, who believe independence has left too much power with Europeans, part-Samoans and foreign advisers.

They demand Samoan control of land, trade and the public service, the end of the separate Individual Voters' Roll, and limits on foreign firms leasing land. They are pro-church and anti-communist but resent Wellington's continuing influence. Their leverage lies in populist appeals to the memory of the Mau, which still stirs strong feeling in the villages.

21.name: Toa o le Atunu'u
21.text:
Toa o le Atunu'u is the hard edge of chiefly nationalism: young titled men and village enforcers who believe Samoa needs discipline imposed from above. They draw on the warrior traditions of the nineteenth-century civil wars and on the power of village councils to punish, fine and banish those who defy them.

They want a single national hierarchy of chiefs commanding obedience, the suppression of dissenting churches and outside ideas, and the expulsion of foreign influence. They despise parliamentary bargaining. They have no organisation and no recognised leader, but in a country where villages already police themselves, their methods are close at hand.

22.name: Western Samoa Police Force
22.text:
Western Samoa has no army, and the Western Samoa Police Force is the only armed body of the state. A small force under the Minister of Police keeps order in Apia, patrols Upolu and Savai'i, and relies heavily on village councils to settle disputes in the countryside. New Zealand trains its officers and would be asked to assist in any emergency.

The force is loyal, conservative and politically quiet, but its commanders believe firmly in order and the authority of the state. Should the matai consensus break down or riots erupt in Apia, it is the only instrument a government could use. Its leverage is small but uniquely armed.

23.name: O le Ao o le Malo
23.english: O le Ao o le Malo
23.native_full: O le Ao o le Malo
23.text:
O le Ao o le Malo, the Head of State, is the highest office of Western Samoa and the pinnacle of its chiefly order. At independence it was entrusted jointly for life to two Tama-a-Aiga, holders of the paramount titles; Malietoa Tanumafili II has held it alone since the death of Tupua Tamasese Mea'ole in 1963.

The office embodies a form of elective monarchy rooted in fa'a Samoa: national unity, continuity of the great titles and the moral authority of the Christian chiefly order. It assents to laws and appoints the prime minister. Its leverage is symbolic but immense, and the other paramount families watch the eventual succession closely.
